1.note: Qoheleth is using **I gave to my heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I thought carefully about.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I carefully considered]

Qoheleth is using the adjectives **righteous** and **wise** as nouns to mean people who are righteous and people who are wise. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [the righteous people and the wise people]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **love** and **hate**, you could express the same ideas in another way. This also occurs in verse 6. Alternate translation: [Whether someone will love them or hate them]

Here, **to their faces** represents “ahead of them,” that is, in their future. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [both are in their future]

2.note: The standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “Everything.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “vapor” and place that word at the end of the previous verse. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

The implication is that the **one happening** that comes to everyone is death. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the one event of death]

2.q: לַ⁠צַּדִּ֤יק וְ⁠לָ⁠רָשָׁע֙ לַ⁠טּוֹב֙ וְ⁠לַ⁠טָּה֣וֹר וְ⁠לַ⁠טָּמֵ֔א וְ⁠לַ⁠זֹּבֵ֔חַ וְ⁠לַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֖ר אֵינֶ֣⁠נּוּ זֹבֵ֑חַ
2.note: Qoheleth is referring to all kinds of people by naming pairs of major components that are opposites, such as **the righteous person** and **the wicked person**, **the pure person** and **the unclean person**, and **the person who sacrifices** and **the person who does not sacrifice**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for every kind of person, whether they are righteous or wicked, good and pure or unclean, whether they sacrifice or do not sacrifice]

The standard written Hebrew text as we have it today reads “for the good person and for the pure person.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “for the good person and for the evil person and for the pure person.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [As it is for the good person, so it is for the sinner; in the same way, as it is for the person who swears an oath, he]

The implication is that **the person who swears** an oath is someone who makes oaths carelessly, while **the person who fears an oath** is someone who respects oaths so much that he is careful about making them. Qoheleth means that the same thing happens to both kinds of people. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the person who carelessly swears an oath is as the person who is careful about making oaths]

3.note: See how you translated this phrase in 1:13. This also occurs in verse 6.
See how you translated **under the sun** in 1:3. This also occurs in verses 6, 9, 11, and 13.

3.q: לֵ֣ב בְּֽנֵי הָ֠⁠אָדָם מָלֵא רָ֨ע וְ⁠הוֹלֵל֤וֹת בִּ⁠לְבָבָ⁠ם֙
3.note: Qoheleth is speaking as if **the heart** of people were a container that is **full of evil** and that has **madness** in it. He means that people constantly think about and desire evil and foolish things. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the sons of humanity constantly think about and desire evil things, and they think about foolish things]
See how you translated **the sons of humanity** in 1:13. This also occurs in verse 12.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **madness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what is senseless]

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and after that, they go to the dead]

4.q: מִי֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר יבחר אֶ֥ל כָּל הַ⁠חַיִּ֖ים
4.note: Qoheleth is using **whoever that is joined to all the living** as a common expression of the culture to mean “whoever is still alive.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [whoever is still alive]

The expression **is joined** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whoever belongs]

The phrase **is joined** is a translation of the correction that later Hebrew scribes recommended in the margin of the text. The written Hebrew text has a word with the same letters in a different order, which means “is chosen.” The ULT follows the correction in the margin, and you may want to do the same or follow the reading of the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [is chosen to belong]

4.q: כִּֽי לְ⁠כֶ֤לֶב חַי֙ ה֣וּא ט֔וֹב מִן הָ⁠אַרְיֵ֖ה הַ⁠מֵּֽת
4.note: The implication is that people in this culture despised dogs but considered the **lion** to be a noble and powerful animal. Qoheleth means that even the lowliest person who is alive is better off than the greatest person who has died. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [for even a living dog, which people despise, is better off than the dead lion, which people honor]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hope**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [there is something that he can confidently expect]

5.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reward**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [anything to gain for what they have done]

Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe the **memory** that other people have of those who have died, not the memory that the dead people themselves have. You may wish to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the memory of them]

6.q: גַּ֣ם אַהֲבָתָ֧⁠ם גַּם שִׂנְאָתָ֛⁠ם גַּם קִנְאָתָ֖⁠ם
6.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **love**, **hate**, and **jealousy**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [Even the fact that they loved, hated, and were jealous]

Qoheleth is speaking as if the **love**, **hate**, and **jealousy** of dead people were living things that have **perished**. He means that these feelings have ended. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [already it has ended]

Qoheleth is speaking as if the good things that people can experience in life were a **portion**, that is, a share of property that someone receives. He means that dead people can no longer take part in or enjoy anything that happens in this life. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And there is nothing for them to enjoy]

7.q: לֵ֣ךְ אֱכֹ֤ל בְּ⁠שִׂמְחָה֙ לַחְמֶ֔⁠ךָ וּֽ⁠שֲׁתֵ֥ה בְ⁠לֶב ט֖וֹב יֵינֶ֑⁠ךָ
7.note: These are imperatives, but they communicate encouragement rather than commands. If the imperatives do not communicate encouragement for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates encouragement. Alternate translation: [You should feel free to go and eat your bread with joy and to drink your wine with a good heart]

Qoheleth is using **Go** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Come now.” He is urging people to act, not telling them to leave a place. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Come now]

Qoheleth is using **bread** to represent food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your meals]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [while being joyful]

Here the **heart** represents the place where a person feels emotions. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with a cheerful attitude]

The implication is that by saying **God has already accepted your deeds**, Qoheleth means that God approves of people enjoying their food and wine in this way. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the God has already approved of your enjoying these things]

8.q: יִהְי֥וּ בְגָדֶ֖י⁠ךָ לְבָנִ֑ים וְ⁠שֶׁ֖מֶן עַל רֹאשְׁ⁠ךָ֥ אַל יֶחְסָֽר
8.note: Wearing white clothes and putting oil on the head were symbolic actions by which people showed that they were joyful and celebrating. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [let your clothes be white to show that you are joyful, and do not let oil be lacking on your head as a sign that you are celebrating]

8.q: יִהְי֥וּ בְגָדֶ֖י⁠ךָ לְבָנִ֑ים וְ⁠שֶׁ֖מֶן עַל רֹאשְׁ⁠ךָ֥ אַל יֶחְסָֽר
8.note: Qoheleth is saying what he wants the person he is addressing to do. Follow the decision of your team on how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [wear white clothes, and always put oil on your head]

9.note: Qoheleth is using **See life** as a common expression of the culture to mean “enjoy life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Enjoy life]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:7. Alternate translation: [your brief life]
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:15.
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:22.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **toil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and in what you work hard at]

10.note: Qoheleth is using **Everything that your hand finds to do** as a common expression of the culture to mean “whatever you have the opportunity to do.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Everything that you have the opportunity to do]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **deed**, **scheme of things**, **knowledge**, and **wisdom**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [no one does anything or plans how things work or knows anything or is wise]

Qoheleth is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase **in Sheol where you are going to there**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [in the grave where you are going when you die]

11.q: לֹא֩ לַ⁠קַּלִּ֨ים הַ⁠מֵּר֜וֹץ וְ⁠לֹ֧א לַ⁠גִּבּוֹרִ֣ים הַ⁠מִּלְחָמָ֗ה
11.note: The implication is that **the swift** do not always win **the race** and **the mighty** do not always win **the war**. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [not always do the swift win the race, and not always do the mighty win the war]

Qoheleth is using the adjectives **swift** and **mighty** as nouns to mean people who are swift and people who are mighty. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [to people who are swift is the race and not to people who are mighty is]

The phrase **a time and the occurrence** expresses a single idea. The word **occurrence** tells more about **time**. Qoheleth means a time when something happens unexpectedly. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [an unexpected time]

12.q: גַּם֩ לֹֽא יֵדַ֨ע הָ⁠אָדָ֜ם אֶת עִתּ֗⁠וֹ
12.note: Qoheleth is not referring to a specific person by **his**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people do not even know their time]

The implication is that **his time** refers to the time when a person will die or when disaster will come upon him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the time when he will die or when disaster will come upon him]

12.q: כַּ⁠דָּגִים֙ שֶׁ⁠נֶּֽאֱחָזִים֙ בִּ⁠מְצוֹדָ֣ה רָעָ֔ה וְ⁠כַ֨⁠צִּפֳּרִ֔ים הָ⁠אֲחֻז֖וֹת
12.note: The expression **are caught** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the ideas in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Like the fish that people catch in a net and like the birds that hunters trap]

The expression **are snared** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the sons of humanity fall into a snare]

Qoheleth is using **when it falls upon them suddenly** as a common expression of the culture to mean “when misfortune happens to them unexpectedly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when it happens to them unexpectedly]

13.note: The pronoun **this** refers to the example of **Wisdom** that Qoheleth describes in the next two verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I saw the following example of wisdom under the sun]

Qoheleth is using **great it was to me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “it impressed me greatly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it impressed me greatly]

14.note: Here the masculine term **men** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and a few people]

15.note: The pronoun **he** refers to someone who **found** the poor wise man. This could mean: (1) the king from the previous verse found this man in the city, Alternate translation: [And the king found in it] or (2) an unspecified person found this man in the city. Alternate translation: [And there was found in it]. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.

The implication is that the **wisdom** of the poor wise man was able to save the city from the king. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and he himself delivered the city from the king by giving wise advice]
See how you translated the similar expression in [8:1](ta:08).

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific **person**. He means people in general, so that no one remembered **that poor man**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But no one remembered]

16.q: וְ⁠אָמַ֣רְתִּי אָ֔נִי טוֹבָ֥ה חָכְמָ֖ה מִ⁠גְּבוּרָ֑ה וְ⁠חָכְמַ֤ת הַ⁠מִּסְכֵּן֙ בְּזוּיָ֔ה וּ⁠דְבָרָ֖י⁠ו אֵינָ֥⁠ם נִשְׁמָעִֽים
16.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [And I said that wisdom is better than might, but the wisdom of the poor person is despised, and his words are not heard]

Qoheleth is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **said** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that this is his own conclusion. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And I myself said]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wisdom** and **might**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [Better is it to be wise than to be strong]

The expression **{is} despised** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but people despise the wisdom of the poor person]

The expression **they are not heard** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people do not listen to his words]

17.q: דִּבְרֵ֣י חֲכָמִ֔ים בְּ⁠נַ֖חַת נִשְׁמָעִ֑ים מִ⁠זַּעֲקַ֥ת מוֹשֵׁ֖ל בַּ⁠כְּסִילִֽים
17.note: Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to show that the quiet words of wise people are more valuable than the shouting of a ruler who leads foolish people. Translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Alternate translation: [People listen more to the quiet words of the wise than to the shouting of a ruler over fools]

The expression **are heeded** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People heed the words of wise people in quietness]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **quietness**, you could express the same idea in another way. This could mean: (1) that wise people who speak their words quietly are heeded, Alternate translation: [spoken quietly] or (2) that people listen calmly to the words of a wise person. Alternate translation: [calmly]

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [more than the cry of a ruler among the fools is heeded]

Qoheleth is using the adjective translated as **fools** as a noun to mean people who are foolish. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [among foolish people]
